title: Source Library Appendix — Detailed Citations and Bias Methodology in Practice
startHere:
*A Shadewater Labs Project — by Alex Yesilcimen with Brine (AI co-author)*

The guide has been promising at the end of every chapter that detailed citations appear here. This appendix delivers on that promise and does one additional thing: it organizes sources by the bias categories the guide has been using throughout, so the appendix doubles as a worked example of the methodology in action. Readers can see how sources cluster by lean, verification status, and institutional position.

The appendix is organized into ten sections:

**A. Canadian Government — Strategy, Policy, and Operational Documents.** Federal framing, operational, and leaked documents. Lean: toward justifying current policy at the framing layer, lower lean at the operational layer.

**B. Canadian Legislation and Provincial Frameworks.** Federal and provincial statutes. Lean: institutional rather than advocacy-positioned, but the choice of what to legislate is itself political.

**C. Provincial Grid Operators and Utility Frameworks.** Operational disclosures from provincial electricity authorities. Lean: technical/operational rather than advocacy.

**D. Canadian Civil Society, Labour, and Advocacy.** Union, creator, civil-liberties, and public-interest organization documentation. Lean: toward the constituency the organization represents. Underlying evidence is often independently strong.

**E. Indigenous-led Frameworks and Research.** Primary frameworks and research from Indigenous-led organizations. The guide treats these as authoritative within their own frames and explicit about the guide's non-Indigenous-led status.

**F. Academic and Peer-Reviewed Research.** Journal articles, conference proceedings, peer-reviewed reports. Lean: toward what the discipline counts as rigour, which is itself a value commitment.

**G. Industry / Corporate Self-Disclosure.** Sustainability reports, technical disclosures, ethics frameworks, commissioned research. Lean: toward the company's interests, even when technically honest.

**H. International Frameworks and Foreign Legislation.** Treaties, foreign statutes, multilateral coordination instruments. Lean: institutional, but the choice of which to engage is policy.

**I. Litigation and Legal Cases.** Court filings and decisions. Lean: party-positioned in pleadings, more neutral in judicial reasoning.

**J. Investigative Journalism and Mainstream Press.** Reporting and analysis from journalism sources. Lean: toward the outlet's editorial position. Evidence often independently verifiable.

Within each section, entries are listed alphabetically by author or organization name. URLs are provided where stable and known; where a stable URL is not available, the entry indicates where the source can be located (publisher, archive, organizational website).

**What this appendix is not.** It is not exhaustive. The guide cited additional sources in passing that are not catalogued here when those citations were not load-bearing for the guide's analysis. It is not always current — URLs change, organizational structures change, documents move. Readers verifying specific claims should be prepared to navigate to current versions of cited material. It is not a substitute for engaging the primary sources directly; the guide's value is in helping readers read primary sources more analytically, not in replacing them.

**What this appendix is.** A comprehensive list of the sources the guide's analysis actually relied on, organized for findability and for transparency about which categories the guide leans on most heavily. Readers who want to verify any specific claim should be able to find the underlying source here.

sections.heading: A. Canadian Government — Strategy, Policy, and Operational Documents
sections.markdown:
**AI for All strategy launch.** Prime Minister's Office press release, ministerial speeches, and strategy backgrounder published June 4, 2026 at Toronto General Hospital. Available at canada.ca and pm.gc.ca. The principal federal AI strategy document for the period this guide covers.

**Algorithmic Impact Assessment tool.** Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat operational instrument supporting the Directive on Automated Decision-Making. Available at canada.ca. The technical assessment framework federal departments use before deploying automated decision systems.

**Bank of Canada Monetary Policy Report.** December 2025 edition. Available at bankofcanada.ca. Contains the analytical section on AI's macroeconomic implications concluding that aggregate unemployment metrics did not yet show widespread AI-driven displacement.

**Bill C-16 — An Act to amend the Criminal Code and other Acts (Protecting Victims Act).** Tabled in the House of Commons by Justice Minister Sean Fraser on December 9, 2025. 158 pages. Available at parl.ca. Addresses femicide classification, coercive control, and synthetic intimate images including AI-generated deepfakes through Criminal Code Section 162.1 amendments.

**Bill C-27 / Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) documentation.** Introduced 2022 as Part 3 of Bill C-27 alongside the Consumer Privacy Protection Act and Personal Information and Data Protection Tribunal Act. Parliamentary committee study materials, government technical companion documents, and ministerial statements. Died on the House floor with the January 2025 prorogation. Available at parl.ca and through Library of Parliament archives.

**CBC News leaked draft of AI for All.** "Inside the draft of Canada's national AI strategy" by Lopez Steven and McKenna, published June 1, 2026 (three days before the official launch). The CBC source remains the primary record of the draft-to-final gap. Available at cbc.ca.

**Federal AI Strategy consultation summary.** ISED publication of consultation outputs (February 2026). Documents the 11,300+ public submissions and 32 expert reports that informed *AI for All*. Available at ised-isde.canada.ca.

**Federal Budget 2024.** Department of Finance Canada. Available at budget.canada.ca. Includes the C$2.4 billion AI package — within it the C$2-billion sovereign-compute commitment whose SME-access slice is the C$300-million AI Compute Access Fund — that became operational under *AI for All*.

**ISED Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems.** Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, launched September 2023 with subsequent signatory additions. Available at ised-isde.canada.ca. Original signatories include Ada, BlackBerry, Cohere, Coveo, OpenText, and TELUS; CGI, IBM, Mastercard, Salesforce, and others joined subsequently — 46 organizations as of June 2026. Microsoft is not a signatory as of that date.

**Minister Evan Solomon Montréal amplification speech.** Speech at Mila in Montréal on June 5, 2026 formalizing the six-pillar structure of *AI for All*. Available through ministerial communications and BetaKit coverage.

**Natural Resources Canada, Best Practice Guide for Canadian Data Centres.** Published November 2024. Available at natural-resources.canada.ca. The federal government's own technical reference documenting the 22% Canadian PUE reporting rate, AI growth projections (1.4% → 2.1% in two years), and Canadian climate advantages for free-air cooling.

**Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada — guidance documents and investigations.** OPC AI-specific guidance, joint findings on Clearview AI (February 2021, with provincial counterparts), Tim Hortons app investigation (2022), and other documented investigations. 2024-25 privacy opinion research documenting 88% concern about AI training data use and 28% Big Tech trust. 2025-26 business survey. Available at priv.gc.ca.

**Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy.** Launched 2017, renewed 2021 with $443 million commitment. The world's first national AI strategy. Documents available through CIFAR and federal AI strategy pages. Established Canada CIFAR AI Chairs, Mila/Vector/Amii institutional structure.

**Statistics Canada AI surveys and analyses.** Survey of Digital Technology and Internet Use, Labour Force Survey, and specific analytical papers on AI and employment published 2024-2026. Documents the 6.1% (Q2 2024) → 12.2% (Q2 2025) → 19.2% (May 2026) adoption trajectory and the 31%/29% labour displacement findings. Available at statcan.gc.ca. The 2025 Federal Budget committed $25M over six years to StatCan's Artificial Intelligence and Technology Measurement Program.

**Treasury Board AI Register.** Launched November 28, 2025 by Treasury Board President Shafqat Ali. Discloses 400+ AI systems across 42 federal institutions, with 1994 as the documented anchor for federal AI use. Available at canada.ca. Searchable, filterable, downloadable in machine-readable format.

**Treasury Board AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service.** Internal-use track distinct from *AI for All*. Available at canada.ca.

**Treasury Board Directive on Automated Decision-Making.** Federal directive establishing requirements for automated decision systems used in federal services. Available at canada.ca. Operates without new legislation through Treasury Board authority over federal procurement and operations.

sections.heading: B. Canadian Legislation and Provincial Frameworks
sections.markdown:
**Alberta Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA).** Provincial private-sector privacy statute. Available at alberta.ca.

**British Columbia Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA), Section 33.1.** Governs disclosure of personal information outside Canada by public bodies. Earlier blanket prohibition repealed in 2021; current framework permits offshore disclosure under specific conditions. Available at bclaws.gov.bc.ca.

**British Columbia Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA).** Provincial private-sector privacy statute. Available at bclaws.gov.bc.ca.

**Canada Elections Act.** Federal statute. Available at laws-lois.justice.gc.ca. Section 91 addresses false statements about candidates affecting voting outcomes.

**Constitution Act, 1867 (Canada).** Foundational federalist allocation of jurisdictional authority between federal Parliament and provincial legislatures. Available at laws-lois.justice.gc.ca. Relevant for the Chapter 15 federalist constraint analysis.

**Copyright Act of Canada.** Federal statute. Available at laws-lois.justice.gc.ca. Sections 3, 27, 29 (fair dealing), and 30.71 (text and data mining for research) are relevant for the Chapter 11 IP analysis.

**Manitoba Bill 51 — public-sector AI and cybersecurity governance framework.** Provincial legislation advancing through the Manitoba legislature. Available at gov.mb.ca.

**Nova Scotia Personal Information International Disclosure Protection Act (PIIDPA).** Provincial statute requiring public bodies and municipalities to keep personal information in Canada unless specific statutory exceptions apply. The clearest provincial public-sector data residency rule documented in the guide. Available at novascotia.ca.

**Online News Act (Canada, 2023).** Federal statute requiring digital platforms to negotiate compensation with Canadian news publishers. Prompted Meta's 2023 block of Canadian news on Facebook and Instagram. Available at laws-lois.justice.gc.ca.

**Ontario Enhancing Digital Security and Trust Act (EDSTA).** In force 2025, pairs AI governance with cybersecurity at public-sector level. March 2026 modernization proposals extend the framework. Available at ontario.ca.

**Ontario Responsible Use of AI Directive.** Provincial directive governing public-service AI deployment. Available at ontario.ca.

**Ontario Working for Workers Act.** Provincial legislation effective January 1, 2026, requiring employers with 25+ employees to disclose AI use in hiring screening. Available at ontario.ca.

**Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA).** Federal private-sector privacy law, drafted in 2000. The OPC has been issuing AI-specific guidance interpreting PIPEDA, but the underlying statute does not contain AI-specific provisions. Available at laws-lois.justice.gc.ca.

**Quebec Act respecting the rights of action against persons distributing intimate images.** Civil regime for non-consensual sharing of intimate images including AI-generated synthetic images. Penalties up to CA$5,000/day for individuals and CA$50,000/day for legal persons. Available at legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca.

**Quebec Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (Law 25).** Passed September 2021 with implementation phased through 2024. Provides Canadian baseline for automated decision rights, privacy impact assessment requirements, mandatory breach notification, and significant financial penalties for non-compliance. Available at legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca.

sections.heading: C. Provincial Grid Operators and Utility Frameworks
sections.markdown:
**Alberta Electric System Operator (AESO).** 2025 large-load queue documentation showing 29 proposed data-centre projects totaling more than 16 GW. AESO imposed 1,200 MW interim large-load connection cap. Documents available at aeso.ca.

**BC Hydro competitive allocation framework.** First two-year call setting aside 300 MW for AI projects and 100 MW for data centres. Permanent exclusion of cryptocurrency-mining loads. Documents available at bchydro.com.

**Canada Energy Regulator (CER).** Provincial generation profiles, market snapshots, and 2023 hydropower variability documentation showing Quebec exports declining from 25.9 TWh (2019) to 13.3 TWh (2023) amid lower precipitation. Available at cer-rec.gc.ca.

**Hydro-Québec.** Large-power tariff regime for 5 MW+ customers. Proposed dedicated large-data-centre tariff (2026). Documents available at hydroquebec.com.

**Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) Ontario.** Data-centre demand projections (13% of new electricity demand by 2035, 4% of total). Documents available at ieso.ca. Ontario reached 145.6 TWh of demand in 2025.

**Uptime Institute Global Data Center Survey 2024.** Industry survey providing 1.56 PUE benchmark and 71% global PUE reporting rate that the guide contrasts with Canada's 22%. Available at uptimeinstitute.com.

sections.heading: D. Canadian Civil Society, Labour, and Advocacy
sections.markdown:
**Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists (ACTRA) AI Submission Explainer (2024).** Position paper documenting 28,000+ Canadian performer constituency and 98%/93% internal survey findings on AI concern. Available at actra.ca.

**ACTRA Independent Production Agreement (IPA) ratified January 21, 2025.** First Canadian collective agreement with explicit AI provisions for performers. Available through ACTRA. Prohibits use of performer recordings for "machine learning" and synthesized performances without consent.

**BC + AI coalition.** "AI for All Has To Mean All of Us" published June 5, 2026 by Kris Krüg with contributions from Indigenous knowledge holders, technologists, and public-interest researchers. Available at bcandai.ca. The principal Canadian civil-society response document to *AI for All*.

**Canadian Civil Liberties Association.** Documentation on AI in policing, surveillance, and civil rights. Available at ccla.org.

**Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and PSP Investments disclosures.** Public disclosures of investment positions, including PSP's lead position in Cohere's 2024 round and CPP Investments' substantial American technology-sector exposure. Available at cppinvestments.com and investpsp.com.

**Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) Senate Brief on Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Workplaces.** March 2026 submission to the Senate Social Affairs Committee, primary researcher Sarah Ryan, 11 pages. The most-detailed Canadian labour primary documentation on AI policy. Documents its 800,000-member constituency (the union's own figure) and five specific legal recommendations. Available at cupe.ca.

**Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI) analyses.** "Canada must do more to protect women and girls from harmful deepfakes" (December 2025) and related analyses on likeness rights and deepfake legislation. Available at cigionline.org.

**Directors Guild of Canada (DGC) parliamentary testimony.** Joint testimony with ACTRA and Music Canada to the Bill C-27 parliamentary committee, February 12, 2024 (INDU meeting 110). DGC National Executive Director Dave Forget proposed three EU AI Act-derived requirements. Available through DGC and parliamentary committee records.

**Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada — additional materials.** Investigation findings, AI guidance documents, and 2024-25 privacy opinion research. Available at priv.gc.ca. The 88%/42%/28%/12% public-opinion polling is documented in the OPC's 2024-25 privacy opinion research.

**Policy Options "U.S. Proxy Lobbying Threatens Canada's Digital Sovereignty"** (November 2025). Civil society analysis of foreign tech corporation lobbying through Canadian intermediaries. Available at policyoptions.irpp.org.

**Quebec Commission d'accès à l'information.** Provincial privacy regulator with substantial enforcement authority under Law 25. Available at cai.gouv.qc.ca.

**Writers' Union of Canada (TWUC).** Position page on AI (writersunion.ca/advocacy/artificial-intelligence) and January 2024 submission to the ISED Copyright in the Age of Generative AI consultation. Documents the position that AI training without permission constitutes copyright infringement under existing Canadian law. Chair Danny Ramadan's public statements on negotiated licensing pathways.

sections.heading: E. Indigenous-led Frameworks and Research
sections.markdown:
**Abundant Intelligences research program.** Co-led from Concordia University and Massey University in Aotearoa New Zealand, with pods including the University of Lethbridge, Bard College, and the University of Hawai'i at West O'ahu. Funded through a more-than-$22M New Frontiers of Research Fund Transformation grant. Documentation available through participating institutions and the New Frontiers of Research Fund.

**First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC) — Ownership, Control, Access, and Possession (OCAP) Principles.** Available at fnigc.ca. Foundational First Nations data sovereignty framework with associated certification infrastructure.

**Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA) — CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance.** Available at gida-global.org. International Indigenous data sovereignty framework: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics. Authors include Tahu Kukutai and Maui Hudson.

**Indigenous Protocol and AI Position Paper (2020).** Polyphonic collection of Indigenous-led contributions including essays, art, fiction, and design protocols. Contributors include Suzanne Kite (Oglála Lakȟóta, "How to Build Anything Ethically"), Hēmi Whaanga (Māori, "AI: a new (r)evolution or the new colonizer for Indigenous peoples?"), and other Indigenous researchers and practitioners. Edited by Jason Edward Lewis. Available through the project website and host institutions.

**Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK) — National Inuit Strategy on Research (NISR, 2018).** Available at itk.ca. Inuit-led research governance framework. Natan Obed authored the foreword. Includes provisions for AI applications involving Inuit data.

**Lewis, Whaanga & Yolgörmez, "Abundant intelligences: placing AI within Indigenous knowledge frameworks."** AI & Society 40(1):2141–2157, 2024. Available through Springer. The academic paper articulating the "AI epistemology problem, not AI ethics problem" framing that organizes the guide's analytical methodology.

**New Frontiers of Research Fund Transformation grant.** More-than-$22M federal grant supporting the Abundant Intelligences program. Documentation available at sshrc-crsh.gc.ca. Significant federal commitment to Indigenous-led AI research that runs in parallel to *AI for All*.

sections.heading: F. Academic and Peer-Reviewed Research
sections.markdown:
**Acemoglu, Daron. "The Simple Macroeconomics of AI."** NBER Working Paper 32487, April 2024. Published in Economic Policy 40(121):13–58, 2025. Available at nber.org. Provides the quantitative framework estimating AI macroeconomic effects at modest scale (~0.5% TFP over ten years) with significant distributional implications.

**Acemoglu, Daron and Simon Johnson.** *Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity.* Public Affairs, 2023. The historical argument that technological progress does not automatically translate into broad-based prosperity absent institutional constraints.

**Acemoglu, Daron, Simon Johnson, and David Autor. "Can we have pro-worker AI?"** CEPR Policy Insight 123, 2023. Available at cepr.org. Joint constructive analysis on pro-worker AI policy.

**Autor, David. "Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs."** NBER Working Paper 32140, 2024. Available at nber.org. The case that generative AI could augment mid-skill expert work rather than only displacing routine work — reversing decades of labour-market polarization.

**Autor, David and Neil Thompson. "Expertise."** NBER Working Paper 33941, 2025. Available at nber.org. Empirical findings on AI effects on within-occupation skill gaps.

**Buolamwini, Joy and Timnit Gebru. "Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification."** Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 2018. Available at proceedings.mlr.press. Foundational documentation of disparate accuracy rates in commercial facial recognition systems.

**Canadian Election Deepfakes 2025.** "Deepfakes in the 2025 Canadian Election: Prevalence, Partisanship, and Platform Dynamics." Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026, also available at arxiv.org/abs/2512.13915. Empirical study documenting 5.9% deepfake rate, partisan asymmetry (9.24% right vs 3.9% left), mostly benign content, 0.1% reach for harmful subset.

**Chouldechova, Alexandra. "Fair prediction with disparate impact: A study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments."** FAccT 2017. Available at proceedings.mlr.press. Foundational algorithmic fairness work establishing the multiple-incompatible-fairness-definitions finding alongside Kleinberg et al.

**Craig, Carys. ISED submission, 2024.** SSRN 4718941. Available at ssrn.com. Detailed Canadian academic submission on copyright and AI training arguing for text-and-data-mining exception with associated protections.

**Craig, Carys.** Chapter in Florian Martin-Bariteau and Teresa Scassa, *AI and Copyright*, 2021. Available through Irwin Law and through academic libraries.

**Geist, Michael. January 2024 ISED consultation submission and subsequent academic writing.** Available at michaelgeist.ca. Detailed analysis arguing that Canadian copyright already permits text-and-data mining through fair dealing as expanded by the 2012 Supreme Court pentalogy, and arguing for explicit TDM exception modelled on EU framework.

**Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville.** *Deep Learning.* MIT Press, 2016. Available at deeplearningbook.org. Foundational technical text on the neural network architectures underlying current AI systems.

**International Energy Agency (IEA). World Energy Outlook 2024.** Available at iea.org. Documents 415 TWh global data-centre electricity in 2024 and projects ~945 TWh by 2030 in base case.

**Kleinberg, Jon, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Manish Raghavan. "Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores."** ITCS 2017. Available at arxiv.org/abs/1609.05807. Foundational mathematical impossibility result showing multiple intuitive definitions of fairness are mutually incompatible in many real-world scenarios.

**Legg, Shane and Marcus Hutter. "Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence."** Minds and Machines 17(4):391-444, 2007. The foundational AGI definition the guide analyzes in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2.

**Li, Pengfei et al. "Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models."** 2023. Available at arxiv.org. Foundational AI water consumption research providing the 10-50 GPT-3 queries per half-litre estimate.

**Livernoche et al. OpenFake dataset documentation.** 2025. Foundational dataset for the 2025 Canadian Election Deepfakes study, containing over 3 million real images paired with approximately 1 million synthetic counterparts.

**Luccioni, Sasha, Emma Strubell, and Kate Crawford. "From Efficiency Gains to Rebound Effects: The Problem of Jevons' Paradox in AI's Polarized Environmental Debate."** FAccT 2025 / arxiv.org/abs/2501.16548. The principal academic counter-framing to corporate AI environmental claims via the Jevons paradox analysis.

**NIST Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT).** Ongoing series of facial recognition system evaluations from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Available at nist.gov/programs-projects/face-recognition-vendor-test-frvt. Documents disparate accuracy rates across demographic groups.

**Obermeyer, Ziad et al. "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations."** Science 366(6464):447–453, 2019. Available at science.org. Foundational documentation of structural bias in US healthcare risk-prediction through proxy choice (healthcare spending as proxy for healthcare need).

**O'Brien (2024).** Academic estimate that real greenhouse gas footprints of major tech-company data centres may exceed reported values by over 600% due to renewable energy certificate accounting. Cited via Luccioni et al. (2025).

**Owen, John R., Deanna Kemp, Éléonore Lèbre, Kamila Svobodova, and Guillermo Pérez Murillo. "Energy transition minerals and their intersection with land-connected peoples."** Nature Sustainability, 2023. Available at nature.com. The 54% finding on energy-transition-mineral projects located on or near Indigenous and peasant lands, which anchors the guide's through-line (the guide's extension of the finding to AI hardware is flagged wherever it appears) on physical-substance extraction geography.

**Shumailov, Ilia et al. "AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data."** Nature, 2024. Available at nature.com. Foundational research on model collapse from training on AI-generated data.

**Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM) — Foundation Model Transparency Index.** Annual publication 2023, 2024, 2025. Available at crfm.stanford.edu/fmti. The centerpiece longitudinal evidence on industry transparency direction, documenting 17-point aggregate decline from 2024 to 2025 across 13 major foundation model developers.

**Tomlinson, Bill, Rebecca Black, David Patterson, and Andrew Torrance. "The carbon emissions of writing and illustrating are lower for AI than for humans."** Scientific Reports, 2024. Available at nature.com. The principal contrarian empirical claim on AI environmental analysis (130-1500× lower CO₂e per page) that the guide engages honestly.

**UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024.** Available at globalewaste.org. Documents 62 million tonnes of e-waste generated globally in 2022, projected 82 million tonnes by 2030, 22% formal collection rate.

**Vaswani, Ashish et al. "Attention Is All You Need."** NeurIPS 2017. Available at arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762. The foundational technical paper introducing the Transformer architecture. Co-author Aidan Gomez went on to found Cohere in Toronto.

**Wang et al. (2024).** AI-related e-waste projection of 1.2-5 million metric tons annually by 2030. Cited via Luccioni et al. (2025).

sections.heading: G. Industry / Corporate Self-Disclosure
sections.markdown:
**Anthropic Constitutional AI documentation and Responsible Scaling Policy.** Available at anthropic.com. Substantial safety-focused transparency alongside selective disclosure in commercial dimensions.

**ASML public disclosures on EUV lithography.** Available at asml.com. Documentation of the Dutch company providing the extreme ultraviolet lithography systems at the chip supply chain's critical bottleneck.

**Cohere corporate disclosures and July 2024 Series D coverage.** Available at cohere.com and through funding announcements. July 2024 US$5.5B Series D; ~US$7B after August–September 2025 raises; April 2026 announced merger with Germany's Aleph Alpha at ~US$20B combined valuation (pending close). Investors include Inovia Capital, Index Ventures, NVIDIA, Oracle, Salesforce, Cisco, and round lead PSP Investments. $240M federal commitment to Cohere's compute build-out announced December 2024 (first investment under the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy; capacity via a CoreWeave-built Cambridge, Ontario facility).

**Cologix.** Canadian colocation operator with 22 sites totaling 94 MW and over 1 million square feet, including 12 facilities in Montréal. Available at cologix.com.

**eStruxture.** Largest Canadian colocation provider with facilities in Montréal, Toronto, Calgary, and Vancouver. Available at estruxture.com.

**Google 2024 Environmental Report.** Available at sustainability.google. Documents 48% increase in Google emissions since 2019 attributed to data centre energy consumption.

**Google Cloud Blog, "Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference."** Vahdat and Dean, August 21, 2025. Available at cloud.google.com/blog. The principal corporate AI environmental disclosure (0.24 Wh / 0.03 gCO2e / 0.26 mL per median Gemini text prompt; 33×/44× improvement) with explicit unverified-by-independent-third-party caveat in footnote 2.

**Meta Llama series release documentation.** Available at meta.com and through technical disclosures.

**Microsoft 2024 Environmental Sustainability Report.** Available at microsoft.com/sustainability. Documents 29.1% increase in Microsoft emissions since 2020.

**NVIDIA technical documentation on H100 architecture.** Available at nvidia.com. Documents the chip operational characteristics underlying AI data centre electrical and thermal load.

**Public First, AWS Canada Impact Report.** Commissioned research report on Amazon Web Services' Canadian footprint. Documents $1.4B direct investment supporting $1.1B GVA over five years, and projected $21B by 2037. Available at publicfirst.co. Worked example of the commissioned-research-firm pattern.

**QScale Q01 Lévis campus.** 142 MW marketed capacity with 60 MW expansion phase begun construction June 2026. Operator disclosures available at qscale.com.

**Reddit-Google licensing deal disclosure (2024).** US$60M/year licensing arrangement for AI training data. Public disclosures and securities filings.

**TSMC public disclosures on fabrication.** Available at tsmc.com. Documentation of the Taiwan-based fabrication that produces the chips at the centre of the global AI supply chain.

**Vantage Data Centers.** Operator including 89 MW combined at Montréal III and 86 MW at Québec City. Available at vantage-dc.com.

sections.heading: H. International Frameworks and Foreign Legislation
sections.markdown:
**Australian eSafety Commissioner framework.** Authority over online safety including AI-generated content. Civil penalties up to AU$782,500 per violation; two-year imprisonment for non-consensual sexually explicit deepfake creators. Available at esafety.gov.au.

**Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances (2012, WIPO).** International treaty extending moral rights to audiovisual performers. Canada has neither signed nor acceded; it is not among the contracting parties. Available at wipo.int. Relevant for the ACTRA performer-rights arguments.

**Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (May 2024).** First internationally-binding treaty on AI. **Canada signed February 11, 2025; ratification remains outstanding as of mid-2026 (the EU became the first ratifying party in May 2026; the treaty is not yet in force).** Available at coe.int.

**Denmark Copyright Act amendment on likeness rights (introduced 2025; pending final adoption as of mid-2026).** Draft legislation establishing likeness rights within copyright, with satire/parody/criticism-of-power exceptions and fifty-year post-mortem protection. The most developed legislative precedent for the convergent likeness-rights mechanism the guide identifies.

**European Union Artificial Intelligence Act.** Effective August 1, 2024, with phased implementation through 2026-2027. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. The most-comprehensive AI regulatory framework currently in force globally. Risk-based classification, mandatory conformity assessment, fines up to 7% of global annual turnover (€35 million floor) for prohibited practices.

**European Union Digital Services Act.** Effective 2024. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. Notice-and-action obligations for online platforms including AI-related content moderation transparency.

**European Union recast Energy Efficiency Directive (2023/1791) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364.** Mandatory reporting from EU data centres ≥500 kW installed IT power on PUE, WUE, key efficiency metrics, and waste heat recovery plans. Available at eur-lex.europa.eu.

**European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).** Available at eur-lex.europa.eu. Foundational data protection regulation with rights to be informed about automated decision-making and to explanation for consequential automated decisions.

**G7 Hiroshima AI Process documentation, including the International Code of Conduct for Advanced AI Developers.** October 2023. Available through G7 documentation and ised-isde.canada.ca. Multilateral AI governance coordination framework.

**Japan AI Strategy 2024 and AI Promotion Act.** Available through Japanese government policy documentation. Active regulatory engagement on AI governance.

**OECD AI Principles (2019, updated).** Available at oecd.org. Adopted by Canada and over 40 OECD member states. Non-binding but the most-cited international AI governance framework.

**Singapore PDPA and AI Governance Framework.** Available at pdpc.gov.sg. Coordinated approach with strong sectoral implementation.

**South Korea AI Basic Act and supporting framework.** Available through Korean government policy documentation.

**UK Online Safety Act (2023, in force with phasing through 2025-2026).** Available at gov.uk. Comprehensive online-harms regulation with Ofcom as regulator. Fines up to £18M or 10% of global annual revenue.

**US CHIPS and Science Act (2022).** US$52B subsidy for domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Available at commerce.gov.

**US TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025).** Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes On Websites and Networks Act. 48-hour platform removal requirement for non-consensual intimate images including AI-generated. Available through US Congress documentation.

**Various US state AI laws.** California AB 2839 (2024; political deepfake prohibitions around elections, successor to the sunset AB 730), Texas SB 751 (deepfake fraud provisions), Tennessee ELVIS Act (likeness protection), Illinois AI provisions, Colorado AI Act. Available through respective state legislative documentation.

sections.heading: I. Litigation and Legal Cases
sections.markdown:
**Andersen v. Stability AI.** US litigation involving image-generation model training. Available through US court records.

**Bartz v. Anthropic.** US litigation over foundation-model training data; a June 2025 ruling found training on lawfully acquired books fair use but not the use of pirated copies, and the case settled for US$1.5 billion (final court approval pending as of mid-2026). Available through US court records.

**Canadian newspapers v. OpenAI.** Ontario Superior Court of Justice, case number CV-24-00732231-00CL. Filed November 29, 2024. Plaintiffs: CBC/Radio-Canada, Canadian Press, Torstar, Postmedia, Metroland Media Group, Globe and Mail. Approximately 16.1 million Canadian news works at issue. Ontario jurisdiction confirmed November 27, 2025. Available through Ontario Superior Court records.

**Books3 litigation including Silverman et al. v. OpenAI.** US litigation regarding the Books3 corpus used in foundation model training. Available through US court records.

**Ewert v. Canada (2018 SCC 30).** Supreme Court of Canada decision on the Correctional Service's use of actuarial risk-assessment tools not validated for Indigenous offenders. The leading Canadian case on bias in administrative decision tools.

**New York Times v. OpenAI.** Active US copyright litigation. Available through US court records. (Distinct from the Times' May 2025 licensing agreement with Amazon, which did not resolve this case; the litigation remains active as of mid-2026.)

**Supreme Court of Canada copyright pentalogy (2012).** Five decisions: CCH Canadian v. Law Society of Upper Canada; Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Bell Canada; Alberta (Education) v. Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency; and related cases. Substantially expanded fair dealing in Canadian copyright. Available at scc-csc.lexum.com.

sections.heading: What's not in this appendix
sections.markdown:
Some sources that the guide mentioned briefly or assumed as background but did not engage as primary evidence for specific claims are not catalogued here. Examples include: passing references to widely-known historical AI research (1956 Dartmouth Conference, ELIZA), general AI textbooks beyond Goodfellow/Bengio/Courville, encyclopedia-style references to historical figures, and similar non-load-bearing citations.

Some sources that the guide's analysis implicitly drew on but did not directly cite — particularly the broader civil society literature on platform regulation, the foundational privacy scholarship predating PIPEDA, and the international labour-economics literature beyond Acemoglu/Autor — are also not catalogued here. The guide's bibliography focuses on the sources that did the load-bearing work, not on the longer reading list a serious AI policy reader might want.

The Sources appendix is also not a current-events tracker. URLs change, organizational structures change, documents get moved or archived. Readers verifying specific claims should be prepared to navigate to current versions of cited material. Where a URL is no longer functional, the entry's identification (author/organization/title/year) should still permit location through search or archive.

sections.heading: Links and URL References
sections.markdown:
This section consolidates URLs for the sources the guide cites, organized by the same categories as the appendix above. Stable URLs are provided where known; where a specific deep URL is not stable or not known, the canonical organizational domain is provided so readers can navigate to the current version of the source.

**A note on URL stability.** URLs change. Organizations restructure their sites. Documents get moved into archives, paywalled, or removed. This list reflects best-known URLs at the time of the guide's drafting (June 2026). Readers verifying specific claims years later should expect to navigate via search, archival snapshots (web.archive.org), or organizational successors. The identifying metadata in the entries above (author, title, year, publisher) is durable in a way that URLs are not.

**A second note.** Several sources cited in the guide do not have public web URLs — internal government documents available only via Access to Information requests, parliamentary committee testimony available through Hansard archives, court filings indexed but not freely posted, and similar. Entries are listed with archive or institutional pointers where this is the case. The guide treats absence of a URL as a fact about the source's accessibility, not as a defect in the citation.

sections.heading: A closing methodological note
sections.markdown:
This source library reflects the guide's specific analytical commitments. The categories are organized to make the bias-mapping methodology visible — readers can see how sources cluster by lean, by verification status, by institutional position. The choice of which sources to include and which to leave out is itself an editorial choice, with the guide's lean (skeptical of corporate self-disclosure, sympathetic to civil-society and Indigenous-led frameworks, willing to engage academic-doctrinal disagreement honestly) reflected in what gets centred and what gets background.

Readers who want a different analytical framework will want a different bibliography. The guide's bibliography is one contribution to Canadian AI literacy, not the comprehensive AI policy reading list. Readers should engage other contributions — from Indigenous-led organizations, from labour organizations, from creator organizations, from privacy commissioners, from academic researchers, from investigative journalism, from community education initiatives — alongside this one.

The sources catalogued here did the work the guide relied on. The work they did was real. The framing the guide put around that work is the guide's responsibility, and readers who want to verify whether the framing serves the evidence should engage the sources directly.

— Alex Yesilcimen and Brine
Shadewater Labs
Vancouver, Canada
June 2026
